articles.title: Multiplexing technologies are expanding the role of biomarkers across development stages
articles.text:
Articles Multiplexing technologies are expanding the role of biomarkers across development stages As multiplexing platforms become more scalable and flexible, biomarkers are playing an increasingly central role in both preclinical and clinical decision-making. Written by Paul Rhyne, PhD Paul Rhyne, PhD Paul Rhyne, PhD, serves as senior director and head of scientific solutions at Luminex. He has deep experience in biomarker testing, with previous roles at the Gates Medical Research Institute, View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Gabriela Cristina Garcia-Soto, PhD Gabriela Cristina Garcia-Soto, PhD Gabriela Cristina Garcia-Soto, PhD, serves as a senior field applications scientist at Luminex. She specializes in multiplex assays, helping researchers design, develop, and validate their own biomarker tests. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 8, 2026 | 4 min read Multiplexing is enabling richer biomarker insights across drug development. credit: istock.com/Jian Fan Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 High-performance biomarkers are essential across drug discovery and development, through clinical trials and regulatory review. Historically, biomarker development has been a challenging and cumbersome task, with the result that biopharma scientists often rely on a limited number of well-established biomarkers. But the advent of multiplexing technologies has streamlined the biomarker discovery and characterization process, providing access to a universe of biomarkers that might otherwise have remained out of reach. These tools have made it possible to study dozens or even hundreds of molecules at once, generating reams of data for a more thorough understanding of each prospective marker. With proper vetting, these biomarkers could play important roles in disease characterization, target discovery and validation, analysis of candidate drugs, evaluation of drug performance in preclinical and clinical studies, and selection of clinical trial participants. Collectively, these uses could improve the success rate of advancing therapeutic candidates from concept to clinic, while enabling earlier elimination of low-confidence leads. That’s a tremendous amount of benefit from something as simple as multiplexing technology for biomarker analysis. The ideal platform should allow scalability and flexibility while remaining responsibly cost-effective. The rise of multiplexing Early-stage drug discovery scientists are no strangers to multiplex biomarker assays. These tools have been used for years to elucidate disease biology, identify and characterize novel targets, and define biomarkers for downstream stages of drug development. Multiplexing technologies have been critical in drug discovery for a wide range of therapeutic products, including vaccines, small molecule therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates, among many others. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More Multiplexing assays are increasingly used across the drug development pipeline, from preclinical research through to later-stage development and clinical studies. In preclinical settings, in particular, they enable scientists to generate richer datasets on dosage and toxicology from limited animal models. By querying dozens or even hundreds of markers simultaneously for a more complete view of biology, these assays increase the informational value of each animal used — and may also help reduce the number required in a given study. The same approach is important for early-stage clinical studies, where human samples must be used sparingly, and scientists typically have to scrutinize the potential value of each biological question they ask. More often than not, researchers wind up paring back the number of markers queried at this stage simply because there is not enough sample volume to enable serial testing of each marker. Multiplexing technologies offer an entirely different value proposition, enabling researchers to ask as many questions as they want from a single low-volume sample. For instance, scientists can deploy a broad cytokine panel to adjust dosage levels during Phase 1 or 2 trials. Other classes of biomarkers can be used to flag off-target effects and even predict response to treatment. Even better, all of these large groups of biomarkers can be analyzed in a single multiplexing assay. This technique has been used extensively in vaccine testing studies , where multiplex assays are frequently used to evaluate vaccine induced immune responses . Of course, the advantages of multiplexing biomarkers depend heavily on the chosen technology platform. Broadly, there are two main categories: planar arrays (also known as solid-phase assays) and bead-based assays. Planar arrays typically provide stronger multiplexing capabilities for nucleic acids, with more limited options for protein analysis. Their fixed format also means they cannot be easily modified by adding or removing biomarkers. In contrast, bead-based assays offer greater flexibility, as specific bead sets can be added or removed within the liquid suspension. This adaptability makes them well suited to workflows where assay content may need to change. Bead-based systems can also multiplex hundreds of biomarkers in a single run. How to implement multiplexing technology Even with the opportunity to multiplex 500 different targets, biopharma scientists must be selective about the biomarkers they query during clinical-stage work. Establishing “context of use” is important, as it defines how and why a biomarker will be used . This step also requires a hypothesis about how the biomarker will increase, decrease, or otherwise change as a result of the study, as well as a plan for how that change will inform the current study or future investigations. Continue reading below... Articles DNA synthesis 101: steps, enzymes, and importance Explore the principles, technologies, and applications that enable scientists to design and build DNA for research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. Read More The choice of multiplexing technology depends on the type and number of biomarkers being measured. Protein and other molecular biomarkers can be assessed using planar or bead-based assays, while tumor size requires radiographic methods and physiological endpoints rely on dedicated measurement techniques. All assays must be sufficiently robust not only to detect biomarkers, but also to quantify changes over time. In clinical studies, biomarker panels are typically smaller and more targeted than those used in discovery research. Nevertheless, highly scalable multiplexing platforms can still offer advantages in clinical settings, enabling continuity from early-stage discovery through to clinical studies and reducing the risk of measurement inconsistencies. Because most pharma companies outsource clinical study data collection and analysis to external laboratories, another important point to consider is how specialized that technology is. Multiplexing platforms that are commonly available in contract labs are easier to source partners for, while niche technologies can be limiting if few labs have the required expertise and infrastructure. As a general rule, commercially available biomarker panels are easier for most laboratories to run than custom assays. One final point is that if a biomarker is likely to be needed post-approval, for example as a companion diagnostic, the assay and underlying technology will require regulatory approval or clearance. Considering this early can help avoid costly and complex assay redesign later in development. Biomarker multiplexing has already transformed early-stage drug discovery, and is now poised to deliver similar gains across preclinical and clinical development. This represents a clear opportunity to meaningfully improve the success rate of new drug development. Feb 24, 2026 | 3 min read Investment follows this operational shift as AI moves from pilot to platform. Gemini Download PDF The biotechnology industry is moving past the initial excitement of artificial intelligence (AI) to confront a more complex reality: the transition from isolated digital tools to fully integrated, AI-native discovery systems. According to the 2026 Biotech AI Report from Benchling, the sector has entered a "builder" phase where the most successful organizations are no longer just running pilots. Instead, they are actively reshaping their data environments and organizational structures to make AI a default part of the research and development (R&D) operating model. Jun 8, 2026 | 4 min read Multiplexing is enabling richer biomarker insights across drug development. credit: istock.com/Jian Fan Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 High-performance biomarkers are essential across drug discovery and development, through clinical trials and regulatory review. Historically, biomarker development has been a challenging and cumbersome task, with the result that biopharma scientists often rely on a limited number of well-established biomarkers. But the advent of multiplexing technologies has streamlined the biomarker discovery and characterization process, providing access to a universe of biomarkers that might otherwise have remained out of reach. These tools have made it possible to study dozens or even hundreds of molecules at once, generating reams of data for a more thorough understanding of each prospective marker. With proper vetting, these biomarkers could play important roles in disease characterization, target discovery and validation, analysis of candidate drugs, evaluation of drug performance in preclinical and clinical studies, and selection of clinical trial participants. Collectively, these uses could improve the success rate of advancing therapeutic candidates from concept to clinic, while enabling earlier elimination of low-confidence leads. That’s a tremendous amount of benefit from something as simple as multiplexing technology for biomarker analysis. The ideal platform should allow scalability and flexibility while remaining responsibly cost-effective. The rise of multiplexing Early-stage drug discovery scientists are no strangers to multiplex biomarker assays. These tools have been used for years to elucidate disease biology, identify and characterize novel targets, and define biomarkers for downstream stages of drug development. Multiplexing technologies have been critical in drug discovery for a wide range of therapeutic products, including vaccines, small molecule therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates, among many others. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More Multiplexing assays are increasingly used across the drug development pipeline, from preclinical research through to later-stage development and clinical studies. In preclinical settings, in particular, they enable scientists to generate richer datasets on dosage and toxicology from limited animal models. By querying dozens or even hundreds of markers simultaneously for a more complete view of biology, these assays increase the informational value of each animal used — and may also help reduce the number required in a given study. The same approach is important for early-stage clinical studies, where human samples must be used sparingly, and scientists typically have to scrutinize the potential value of each biological question they ask. More often than not, researchers wind up paring back the number of markers queried at this stage simply because there is not enough sample volume to enable serial testing of each marker. Multiplexing technologies offer an entirely different value proposition, enabling researchers to ask as many questions as they want from a single low-volume sample. For instance, scientists can deploy a broad cytokine panel to adjust dosage levels during Phase 1 or 2 trials. Other classes of biomarkers can be used to flag off-target effects and even predict response to treatment. Even better, all of these large groups of biomarkers can be analyzed in a single multiplexing assay. This technique has been used extensively in vaccine testing studies , where multiplex assays are frequently used to evaluate vaccine induced immune responses . Of course, the advantages of multiplexing biomarkers depend heavily on the chosen technology platform. Broadly, there are two main categories: planar arrays (also known as solid-phase assays) and bead-based assays. Planar arrays typically provide stronger multiplexing capabilities for nucleic acids, with more limited options for protein analysis. Their fixed format also means they cannot be easily modified by adding or removing biomarkers. In contrast, bead-based assays offer greater flexibility, as specific bead sets can be added or removed within the liquid suspension. This adaptability makes them well suited to workflows where assay content may need to change. Bead-based systems can also multiplex hundreds of biomarkers in a single run. How to implement multiplexing technology Even with the opportunity to multiplex 500 different targets, biopharma scientists must be selective about the biomarkers they query during clinical-stage work. Establishing “context of use” is important, as it defines how and why a biomarker will be used . This step also requires a hypothesis about how the biomarker will increase, decrease, or otherwise change as a result of the study, as well as a plan for how that change will inform the current study or future investigations. Continue reading below... Read More The choice of multiplexing technology depends on the type and number of biomarkers being measured. Protein and other molecular biomarkers can be assessed using planar or bead-based assays, while tumor size requires radiographic methods and physiological endpoints rely on dedicated measurement techniques. All assays must be sufficiently robust not only to detect biomarkers, but also to quantify changes over time. In clinical studies, biomarker panels are typically smaller and more targeted than those used in discovery research. Nevertheless, highly scalable multiplexing platforms can still offer advantages in clinical settings, enabling continuity from early-stage discovery through to clinical studies and reducing the risk of measurement inconsistencies. Because most pharma companies outsource clinical study data collection and analysis to external laboratories, another important point to consider is how specialized that technology is. Multiplexing platforms that are commonly available in contract labs are easier to source partners for, while niche technologies can be limiting if few labs have the required expertise and infrastructure. As a general rule, commercially available biomarker panels are easier for most laboratories to run than custom assays. One final point is that if a biomarker is likely to be needed post-approval, for example as a companion diagnostic, the assay and underlying technology will require regulatory approval or clearance. Considering this early can help avoid costly and complex assay redesign later in development. Biomarker multiplexing has already transformed early-stage drug discovery, and is now poised to deliver similar gains across preclinical and clinical development. This represents a clear opportunity to meaningfully improve the success rate of new drug development. High-performance biomarkers are essential across drug discovery and development, through clinical trials and regulatory review. Historically, biomarker development has been a challenging and cumbersome task, with the result that biopharma scientists often rely on a limited number of well-established biomarkers. But the advent of multiplexing technologies has streamlined the biomarker discovery and characterization process, providing access to a universe of biomarkers that might otherwise have remained out of reach. These tools have made it possible to study dozens or even hundreds of molecules at once, generating reams of data for a more thorough understanding of each prospective marker. With proper vetting, these biomarkers could play important roles in disease characterization, target discovery and validation, analysis of candidate drugs, evaluation of drug performance in preclinical and clinical studies, and selection of clinical trial participants. Collectively, these uses could improve the success rate of advancing therapeutic candidates from concept to clinic, while enabling earlier elimination of low-confidence leads. That’s a tremendous amount of benefit from something as simple as multiplexing technology for biomarker analysis. The ideal platform should allow scalability and flexibility while remaining responsibly cost-effective. The rise of multiplexing Early-stage drug discovery scientists are no strangers to multiplex biomarker assays. These tools have been used for years to elucidate disease biology, identify and characterize novel targets, and define biomarkers for downstream stages of drug development. Multiplexing technologies have been critical in drug discovery for a wide range of therapeutic products, including vaccines, small molecule therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates, among many others. Read More Multiplexing assays are increasingly used across the drug development pipeline, from preclinical research through to later-stage development and clinical studies. In preclinical settings, in particular, they enable scientists to generate richer datasets on dosage and toxicology from limited animal models. By querying dozens or even hundreds of markers simultaneously for a more complete view of biology, these assays increase the informational value of each animal used — and may also help reduce the number required in a given study. The same approach is important for early-stage clinical studies, where human samples must be used sparingly, and scientists typically have to scrutinize the potential value of each biological question they ask. More often than not, researchers wind up paring back the number of markers queried at this stage simply because there is not enough sample volume to enable serial testing of each marker. Multiplexing technologies offer an entirely different value proposition, enabling researchers to ask as many questions as they want from a single low-volume sample. For instance, scientists can deploy a broad cytokine panel to adjust dosage levels during Phase 1 or 2 trials. Other classes of biomarkers can be used to flag off-target effects and even predict response to treatment. Even better, all of these large groups of biomarkers can be analyzed in a single multiplexing assay. This technique has been used extensively in vaccine testing studies , where multiplex assays are frequently used to evaluate vaccine induced immune responses . Of course, the advantages of multiplexing biomarkers depend heavily on the chosen technology platform. Broadly, there are two main categories: planar arrays (also known as solid-phase assays) and bead-based assays. Planar arrays typically provide stronger multiplexing capabilities for nucleic acids, with more limited options for protein analysis. Their fixed format also means they cannot be easily modified by adding or removing biomarkers. In contrast, bead-based assays offer greater flexibility, as specific bead sets can be added or removed within the liquid suspension. This adaptability makes them well suited to workflows where assay content may need to change. Bead-based systems can also multiplex hundreds of biomarkers in a single run. How to implement multiplexing technology Even with the opportunity to multiplex 500 different targets, biopharma scientists must be selective about the biomarkers they query during clinical-stage work. Establishing “context of use” is important, as it defines how and why a biomarker will be used . This step also requires a hypothesis about how the biomarker will increase, decrease, or otherwise change as a result of the study, as well as a plan for how that change will inform the current study or future investigations. Read More The choice of multiplexing technology depends on the type and number of biomarkers being measured. Protein and other molecular biomarkers can be assessed using planar or bead-based assays, while tumor size requires radiographic methods and physiological endpoints rely on dedicated measurement techniques. All assays must be sufficiently robust not only to detect biomarkers, but also to quantify changes over time. In clinical studies, biomarker panels are typically smaller and more targeted than those used in discovery research. Nevertheless, highly scalable multiplexing platforms can still offer advantages in clinical settings, enabling continuity from early-stage discovery through to clinical studies and reducing the risk of measurement inconsistencies. Because most pharma companies outsource clinical study data collection and analysis to external laboratories, another important point to consider is how specialized that technology is. Multiplexing platforms that are commonly available in contract labs are easier to source partners for, while niche technologies can be limiting if few labs have the required expertise and infrastructure. As a general rule, commercially available biomarker panels are easier for most laboratories to run than custom assays. One final point is that if a biomarker is likely to be needed post-approval, for example as a companion diagnostic, the assay and underlying technology will require regulatory approval or clearance. Considering this early can help avoid costly and complex assay redesign later in development. Biomarker multiplexing has already transformed early-stage drug discovery, and is now poised to deliver similar gains across preclinical and clinical development. This represents a clear opportunity to meaningfully improve the success rate of new drug development.

Gemini Download PDF The biotechnology industry is moving past the initial excitement of artificial intelligence (AI) to confront a more complex reality: the transition from isolated digital tools to fully integrated, AI-native discovery systems. According to the 2026 Biotech AI Report from Benchling, the sector has entered a "builder" phase where the most successful organizations are no longer just running pilots. Instead, they are actively reshaping their data environments and organizational structures to make AI a default part of the research and development (R&D) operating model. For drug developers, this shift represents a move toward an AI operating system where digital models and laboratory experiments exist in a continuous, closed-loop cycle of discovery. Accelerating the upstream pipeline Drug developers are seeing the most significant AI impact in the early stages of the pipeline, where decisions about targets and constructs set the trajectory for a decade of work. Because drug development typically takes 10 to 12 years, these upstream improvements compound over time; faster cycles and fewer dead ends in the discovery phase matter enormously for long-term return of investment (ROI). According to the report, half of those adopting AI in biotech already report faster time-to-target, and 42 percent see an uplift in accuracy and hit rates with scientific models. Read More Today, predictive models lead adoption because they sit on mature, well-structured datasets. For instance, protein structure prediction is used by 73 percent of leaders, and docking models are used by 52 percent. These "killer apps" succeed because they operate where data is clean and results are easily verifiable. By tightly coupling AI design systems with the lab, researchers are effectively shrinking drug discovery timelines from years to months. Infrastructure bottlenecks Despite these early wins, the industry is hitting a ceiling where AI adoption drops sharply in complex domains like generative design (42 percent adoption), biomarker analysis (40 percent), and ADME prediction (29 percent). The limitation is rarely the models themselves; rather, it is the data environment where information lives across a dozen systems and key metadata is often missing. Poor data quality and availability are cited as the number one reason AI pilots fail, mentioned by 55 percent of organizations. Biology’s data is often too messy or incomplete to teach machines effectively, and as experts note, no amount of retroactive normalization can fix a poorly designed experiment. To break through this ceiling, leaders are investing in "prospective data" — high-quality, well-annotated measurements that models can truly learn from. Organizations with high AI adoption are nearly twice as likely to report strong wet-dry lab integration — 30 percent compared to 18 percent for low adopters — allowing for a data flywheel where insights continually inform decisions and accelerate learning. The rise of the scientific translator The report highlights a fundamental shift in talent strategy: drug developers are building AI expertise at the bench rather than just hiring from the technology sector. Internal upskilling of existing scientific staff is the most common source of AI talent (67 percent citing), far outpacing hiring from tech companies at 21 percent. This stems from a critical need for "scientific translators" — people who can navigate the nuanced intersection of complex biology, regulatory requirements, and machine learning. This shift is reshaping the organizational chart to keep AI close to science. The most common model now places AI leadership directly inside R&D (30 percent) to keep technology tied to experimental context. Additionally, 35 percent of organizations have adopted a hybrid model, pairing a centralized AI group for shared standards with specialists embedded in R&D teams. This proximity to the bench reduces handoffs and ensures that AI tools are usable in the flow of real-world experiments. A new discovery model As AI becomes the standard," biotech is adopting a "build what differentiates, buy what scales" mindset. Roughly 60 percent of teams buy proven commercial components, while 55 percent build or fine-tune models in-house where their proprietary biology is unique. Trust is also maturing into a "trust but verify" phase with 66 percent of scientists reporting an increase in confidence in large language model (LLM) outputs over the past year, though they still rely on domain expertise to decide when an AI hypothesis is worth testing. Investment follows this operational shift as AI moves from pilot to platform. A staggering 80 percent of organizations plan to increase their AI budgets in the next 12 months, with 23 percent expecting to double their spend or more. This capital is being moved into data infrastructure and expanded scientific modeling capabilities. According to NVIDIA’s Healthcare division , the ultimate goal is an interoperable ecosystem where co-scientist agents, multimodal models, and automated workflows coordinate experiments and decisions end-to-end. The biotechnology industry is moving past the initial excitement of artificial intelligence (AI) to confront a more complex reality: the transition from isolated digital tools to fully integrated, AI-native discovery systems.
According to the 2026 Biotech AI Report from Benchling, the sector has entered a "builder" phase where the most successful organizations are no longer just running pilots. Instead, they are actively reshaping their data environments and organizational structures to make AI a default part of the research and development (R&D) operating model.
2026 Biotech AI Report
For drug developers, this shift represents a move toward an AI operating system where digital models and laboratory experiments exist in a continuous, closed-loop cycle of discovery.
Accelerating the upstream pipeline
Drug developers are seeing the most significant AI impact in the early stages of the pipeline, where decisions about targets and constructs set the trajectory for a decade of work. Because drug development typically takes 10 to 12 years, these upstream improvements compound over time; faster cycles and fewer dead ends in the discovery phase matter enormously for long-term return of investment (ROI). According to the report, half of those adopting AI in biotech already report faster time-to-target, and 42 percent see an uplift in accuracy and hit rates with scientific models.
Today, predictive models lead adoption because they sit on mature, well-structured datasets. For instance, protein structure prediction is used by 73 percent of leaders, and docking models are used by 52 percent. These "killer apps" succeed because they operate where data is clean and results are easily verifiable. By tightly coupling AI design systems with the lab, researchers are effectively shrinking drug discovery timelines from years to months.
Infrastructure bottlenecks
Despite these early wins, the industry is hitting a ceiling where AI adoption drops sharply in complex domains like generative design (42 percent adoption), biomarker analysis (40 percent), and ADME prediction (29 percent). The limitation is rarely the models themselves; rather, it is the data environment where information lives across a dozen systems and key metadata is often missing. Poor data quality and availability are cited as the number one reason AI pilots fail, mentioned by 55 percent of organizations.
Biology’s data is often too messy or incomplete to teach machines effectively, and as experts note, no amount of retroactive normalization can fix a poorly designed experiment. To break through this ceiling, leaders are investing in "prospective data" — high-quality, well-annotated measurements that models can truly learn from. Organizations with high AI adoption are nearly twice as likely to report strong wet-dry lab integration — 30 percent compared to 18 percent for low adopters — allowing for a data flywheel where insights continually inform decisions and accelerate learning.
The rise of the scientific translator
The report highlights a fundamental shift in talent strategy: drug developers are building AI expertise at the bench rather than just hiring from the technology sector. Internal upskilling of existing scientific staff is the most common source of AI talent (67 percent citing), far outpacing hiring from tech companies at 21 percent. This stems from a critical need for "scientific translators" — people who can navigate the nuanced intersection of complex biology, regulatory requirements, and machine learning.
This shift is reshaping the organizational chart to keep AI close to science. The most common model now places AI leadership directly inside R&D (30 percent) to keep technology tied to experimental context. Additionally, 35 percent of organizations have adopted a hybrid model, pairing a centralized AI group for shared standards with specialists embedded in R&D teams. This proximity to the bench reduces handoffs and ensures that AI tools are usable in the flow of real-world experiments.
A new discovery model
As AI becomes the standard," biotech is adopting a "build what differentiates, buy what scales" mindset. Roughly 60 percent of teams buy proven commercial components, while 55 percent build or fine-tune models in-house where their proprietary biology is unique. Trust is also maturing into a "trust but verify" phase with 66 percent of scientists reporting an increase in confidence in large language model (LLM) outputs over the past year, though they still rely on domain expertise to decide when an AI hypothesis is worth testing.
Investment follows this operational shift as AI moves from pilot to platform. A staggering 80 percent of organizations plan to increase their AI budgets in the next 12 months, with 23 percent expecting to double their spend or more. This capital is being moved into data infrastructure and expanded scientific modeling capabilities. According to NVIDIA’s Healthcare division , the ultimate goal is an interoperable ecosystem where co-scientist agents, multimodal models, and automated workflows coordinate experiments and decisions end-to-end.

articles.title: Overcoming mixing challenges in high-viscosity bioprocesses
articles.text:
Articles Overcoming mixing challenges in high-viscosity bioprocesses As bioprocess intensification pushes cell densities higher, engineering the right agitation strategy becomes the critical factor separating productive runs from failed batches. Written by Erika Russell Erika Russell Erika Russell, BSc, is a Science Writer and Editor for LabX Media Group. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 5, 2026 | 6 min read Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses demands precise torque, agitation profiles, and impeller selection to maintain mass transfer and culture homogeneity. GEMINI (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 6:00 Highlights in this article Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications CFD modeling as a scale-up tool for viscous bioprocesses Dissolved oxygen control strategies for viscous cultures Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing Thicker, intensified cultures create bigger mass transfer problems, and only precise agitation keeps them in check. When cell densities climb and viscosity rises in fed-batch and perfusion processes, conventional mixing assumptions break down. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses requires a fundamentally different engineering approach, one that accounts for torque limitations, oxygen transfer rates, and shear sensitivity simultaneously. Key takeaways High-viscosity bioprocesses alter fluid dynamics in ways that standard mixing models underestimate. Rising culture viscosity reduces bulk flow velocity and creates stagnant zones that impair nutrient distribution and oxygen transfer, directly threatening cell viability and product quality. Impeller selection and configuration are the primary levers for managing mixing in dense, viscous cultures. Radial-flow and axial-flow impellers each offer distinct trade-offs between shear stress, power consumption, and bulk blending efficiency that must be matched to the specific culture system. The kLa value (the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient) is the practical benchmark for mixing adequacy in high-viscosity systems. Engineering teams that monitor and optimize kLa across scale can predict and prevent the oxygen limitation events that derail intensified runs. Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing Process intensification strategies (including high-density fed-batch, concentrated feeding regimens, and N-1 perfusion seed trains using alternating tangential flow filtration ) consistently push cultures toward rheological conditions that standard bioreactor mixing designs were never optimized to handle. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage. This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More The result is a set of competing engineering pressures that define the core challenge of mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. Lower agitation preserves cell integrity but risks the formation of dead zones where oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients accumulate. The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa). The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel. Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration. Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises. Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing. Continue reading below... Articles DNA synthesis 101: steps, enzymes, and importance Explore the principles, technologies, and applications that enable scientists to design and build DNA for research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. Read More Impeller type Flow pattern Gas dispersion Shear level High-viscosity suitability Rushton turbine Radial Excellent High Moderate (risk of shear damage) Pitched-blade turbine Axial Moderate Low to moderate Good for bulk blending Hydrofoil (e.g., A310 type) Axial Moderate Low Strong for high-density cultures Marine propeller Axial Low Low Limited above moderate viscosity Staged hybrid (radial + axial) Mixed Excellent Variable Preferred for intensified processes Impeller-to-vessel diameter ratio (D/T) is another variable that must be revisited for high-viscosity applications. Published engineering guidance for animal cell culture places the standard D/T range between 0.33 and 0.5, and moving toward the upper end of that range can significantly improve mixing time and reduce zone heterogeneity in viscous cultures. As culture viscosity rises, torque demand increases nonlinearly, so the mechanical drive system must be specified with adequate torque capacity, validated against the worst-case viscosity expected at peak cell density before committing to a vessel configuration. CFD modeling as a scale-up tool for viscous bioprocesses Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has moved from a research tool into a practical engineering resource for bioreactor scale-up, and its value is particularly high for high-viscosity applications where empirical correlations developed for low-viscosity systems can mislead. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth. For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. A mass-transfer modeling study in Biochemical Engineering Journal demonstrated that this approach enabled direct scale-up of a CHO antibody process from 2-L to 1,500-L without intermediate steps, with consistent process performance and product quality across scales. The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start. Dissolved oxygen control strategies for viscous cultures Maintaining dissolved oxygen above the critical threshold becomes progressively more difficult as culture viscosity rises and kLa declines. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. The standard dissolved oxygen control cascade, which increases agitation speed and then increases airflow rate as DO falls, remains the primary control strategy but must be implemented with culture-specific limits to prevent shear damage or excessive CO₂ accumulation from high gas flow rates. Oxygen enrichment of the inlet gas stream (substituting pure oxygen or high-oxygen mixtures for air) is a widely used supplemental strategy for maintaining DO in high-density, high-viscosity cultures. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in the sparged gas, enrichment increases the driving force for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid interface without requiring a proportional increase in gas flow rate, which would otherwise strip CO₂ and drive pH excursions. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone. Continue reading below... Infographics How to run a successful high-throughput screening campaign Learn the key assay design principles and workflow considerations that help support robust, scalable, and reliable high-throughput screening campaigns. Read More Microspargers (spargers with very small pore sizes that generate fine bubbles) increase the gas-liquid interfacial area and improve kLa in viscous cultures, but are more prone to fouling and require higher inlet pressure to overcome surface tension effects at the pore. Combining a microsparger for oxygen transfer with a ring sparger for CO₂ stripping is an approach used in some high-density culture systems to address both gas transfer directions independently. Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses is a system-level engineering challenge that requires integrating rheological characterization, impeller selection, drive system specification, dissolved oxygen control strategy, and CFD-guided scale-up into a coherent process development program. The teams that manage this challenge successfully treat mixing as a first-class process parameter from the earliest stages of intensified process design, rather than as a scale-up problem to be solved after the biological performance has been locked in. For programs moving toward commercial manufacturing, the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities provides a framework for integrating these mixing specifications into facility design from the outset. The increasing adoption of high-density fed-batch and continuous perfusion platforms, and the insights that connect those approaches to the wider discipline of bioprocessing scale-up , make high-viscosity mixing engineering a near-universal challenge for modern biomanufacturing. Investing in rigorous mixing characterization and physically validated CFD modeling during process development is the most reliable way to prevent agitation failures from appearing at commercial scale, where inadequate agitation means lost batches, failed DO control, and irreproducible scale-up. This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines . Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses? Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses refers to the agitation strategies and engineering approaches used to maintain homogeneous culture conditions (including nutrient distribution, dissolved oxygen, and pH uniformity) when culture broth rheology departs from standard low-viscosity conditions due to high cell densities, concentrated feeds, or accumulated metabolites. Why does high cell density increase culture viscosity? Elevated cell density increases the volumetric fraction of suspended biomass in the culture medium and promotes the accumulation of extracellular proteins, polysaccharides, and metabolic byproducts that collectively raise apparent viscosity. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior emerges when these components interact with shear forces during agitation. How does viscosity affect oxygen mass transfer in bioreactors? Increased viscosity reduces the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa) by promoting bubble coalescence, slowing bubble rise velocity, and thickening the liquid film resistance at the gas-liquid interface. The result is impaired oxygen supply to cells, which risks dissolved oxygen limitation and reduced cell productivity. Although regulatory frameworks emphasize quantification, conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR) methods do not distinguish between fragmented DNA and intact sequences with potential biological activity, limiting the depth of risk assessment. This gap has prompted the development of analytical approaches capable of resolving DNA integrity at higher resolution. In this webinar, David Dobnik and Emily Blair will discuss a first-of-its-kind study using single-molecule linkage analysis to evaluate DNA impurity integrity in rAAV products and its implications in quality control and process characterization. Speakers David Dobnik, PhD Assistant Professor National Institute of Biology (NIB) Emily Blair, PhD Senior Project Manager Countable Labs Sponsored by Top Image Credit: iStock: Alena Butusava News You cannot understand biology by killing it Drug discovery still relies on destroying cells to understand how they respond, but new real-time measurement approaches are beginning to reveal biology in motion rather than in snapshots. Written by Bree Foster, PhD Bree Foster, PhD Bree Foster is a science writer at Drug Discovery News with over 2 years of experience at Technology Networks , Drug Discovery News , and other scientific marketing agencies. ​ View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 11, 2026 | 5 min read Cell Cinema, Precigenetic's highest-resolution spatial readout, operates without labels or probes, to create real-time movies of ​living cellular chemistry. credit: Precigenetics Download PDF Modern drug discovery is built on a paradox. To learn how living systems respond to intervention, we routinely destroy them. Cells are lysed, fixed, stained, sequenced, averaged, and reconstructed after the fact. This gives us a snapshot of what the cells were like before and after, but tells us very little about what happened in between. This workflow has become so normalized that its limitations are often treated as facts of life. Drug resistance seems sudden and unexpected, while mechanisms of action can take months to untangle. But these are direct consequences of how we measure biology. A growing group of researchers and technologists are beginning to question this methodology and instead measure biology in real time. In a recent Nature Communications study , researchers used densely sampled, time-resolved measurements to follow cancer cells as they were exposed to targeted therapies. Rather than comparing only baseline and endpoint states, they tracked how gene expression programs and chromatin states evolved across many intermediate timepoints. What emerged was not a smooth transition from sensitive to resistant cells, but a structured progression through intermediate cellular states. Importantly, cells did not drift randomly into resistance; they passed through predictable transitional states in which early molecular changes foreshadowed later survival outcomes. These intermediate cellular states could be prime targets for intervention before full therapeutic resistance is established. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More This type and depth of information is crucial to better understanding disease processes, because it moves the focus away from static classification and toward the dynamics of how systems evolve under pressure. Rather than asking whether a cell is sensitive or resistant, the question becomes how it transitions between these states, and what molecular events govern that transition. Biology is not static However, while this approach is much more informative than traditional endpoint assays, it still has limitations. Each timepoint in these studies is still generated by destroying a population of cells, extracting molecular information, and reconstructing dynamics afterwards. What appears as a continuous trajectory is, in practice, a carefully stitched approximation built from discrete, non-overlapping snapshots. This distinction matters because the most informative biology may occur between the sampled moments. Early metabolic shifts, transient stress responses, and rapidly reversible states can be missed entirely if they do not align with the chosen sampling schedule. In other words, increasing the number of timepoints improves resolution, but does not fundamentally change the fact that the system is still being observed indirectly. This gap between observation and process has led to interest in methods that can remain continuously coupled to living systems, capturing their state without interrupting or resetting it. Rather than treating cells as endpoints to be repeatedly sampled, these approaches aim to treat them as continuously evolving systems that can be measured in place, preserving both their temporal structure and their internal heterogeneity as they respond to perturbation. DDN spoke with Parmita Mishra , founder and CEO of Precigenetics , who is developing a label-free optical platform designed to interrogate living cells continuously at the level of their native chemistry. Instead of relying on fluorescent tags or destructive readouts, the system uses optical signatures of molecular bonds to track changes in proteins, lipids, and metabolites over time within the same intact cells. “The idea is that we use subcellular vibrational spectroscopy — of which Raman imaging is a leading example,” she said. “It’s label-free and already well established in materials science, and even used on Mars rovers to detect chemical signatures that could indicate microbial life. Written by Erika Russell Erika Russell Erika Russell, BSc, is a Science Writer and Editor for LabX Media Group. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . When cell densities climb and viscosity rises in fed-batch and perfusion processes, conventional mixing assumptions break down. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses requires a fundamentally different engineering approach, one that accounts for torque limitations, oxygen transfer rates, and shear sensitivity simultaneously. Key takeaways High-viscosity bioprocesses alter fluid dynamics in ways that standard mixing models underestimate. Rising culture viscosity reduces bulk flow velocity and creates stagnant zones that impair nutrient distribution and oxygen transfer, directly threatening cell viability and product quality. Impeller selection and configuration are the primary levers for managing mixing in dense, viscous cultures. Radial-flow and axial-flow impellers each offer distinct trade-offs between shear stress, power consumption, and bulk blending efficiency that must be matched to the specific culture system. The kLa value (the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient) is the practical benchmark for mixing adequacy in high-viscosity systems. Engineering teams that monitor and optimize kLa across scale can predict and prevent the oxygen limitation events that derail intensified runs. Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing Process intensification strategies (including high-density fed-batch, concentrated feeding regimens, and N-1 perfusion seed trains using alternating tangential flow filtration ) consistently push cultures toward rheological conditions that standard bioreactor mixing designs were never optimized to handle. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage. This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely. Read More The result is a set of competing engineering pressures that define the core challenge of mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. Lower agitation preserves cell integrity but risks the formation of dead zones where oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients accumulate. The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa). The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel. Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration. Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises. Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing. Published engineering guidance for animal cell culture places the standard D/T range between 0.33 and 0.5, and moving toward the upper end of that range can significantly improve mixing time and reduce zone heterogeneity in viscous cultures. As culture viscosity rises, torque demand increases nonlinearly, so the mechanical drive system must be specified with adequate torque capacity, validated against the worst-case viscosity expected at peak cell density before committing to a vessel configuration. CFD modeling as a scale-up tool for viscous bioprocesses Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has moved from a research tool into a practical engineering resource for bioreactor scale-up, and its value is particularly high for high-viscosity applications where empirical correlations developed for low-viscosity systems can mislead. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth. For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. A mass-transfer modeling study in Biochemical Engineering Journal demonstrated that this approach enabled direct scale-up of a CHO antibody process from 2-L to 1,500-L without intermediate steps, with consistent process performance and product quality across scales. The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start. Dissolved oxygen control strategies for viscous cultures Maintaining dissolved oxygen above the critical threshold becomes progressively more difficult as culture viscosity rises and kLa declines. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. The standard dissolved oxygen control cascade, which increases agitation speed and then increases airflow rate as DO falls, remains the primary control strategy but must be implemented with culture-specific limits to prevent shear damage or excessive CO₂ accumulation from high gas flow rates. Oxygen enrichment of the inlet gas stream (substituting pure oxygen or high-oxygen mixtures for air) is a widely used supplemental strategy for maintaining DO in high-density, high-viscosity cultures. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in the sparged gas, enrichment increases the driving force for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid interface without requiring a proportional increase in gas flow rate, which would otherwise strip CO₂ and drive pH excursions. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone. Read More Microspargers (spargers with very small pore sizes that generate fine bubbles) increase the gas-liquid interfacial area and improve kLa in viscous cultures, but are more prone to fouling and require higher inlet pressure to overcome surface tension effects at the pore. Combining a microsparger for oxygen transfer with a ring sparger for CO₂ stripping is an approach used in some high-density culture systems to address both gas transfer directions independently. Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses is a system-level engineering challenge that requires integrating rheological characterization, impeller selection, drive system specification, dissolved oxygen control strategy, and CFD-guided scale-up into a coherent process development program. The teams that manage this challenge successfully treat mixing as a first-class process parameter from the earliest stages of intensified process design, rather than as a scale-up problem to be solved after the biological performance has been locked in. For programs moving toward commercial manufacturing, the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities provides a framework for integrating these mixing specifications into facility design from the outset. The increasing adoption of high-density fed-batch and continuous perfusion platforms, and the insights that connect those approaches to the wider discipline of bioprocessing scale-up , make high-viscosity mixing engineering a near-universal challenge for modern biomanufacturing. Investing in rigorous mixing characterization and physically validated CFD modeling during process development is the most reliable way to prevent agitation failures from appearing at commercial scale, where inadequate agitation means lost batches, failed DO control, and irreproducible scale-up. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses refers to the agitation strategies and engineering approaches used to maintain homogeneous culture conditions (including nutrient distribution, dissolved oxygen, and pH uniformity) when culture broth rheology departs from standard low-viscosity conditions due to high cell densities, concentrated feeds, or accumulated metabolites. Why does high cell density increase culture viscosity? Elevated cell density increases the volumetric fraction of suspended biomass in the culture medium and promotes the accumulation of extracellular proteins, polysaccharides, and metabolic byproducts that collectively raise apparent viscosity. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior emerges when these components interact with shear forces during agitation. How does viscosity affect oxygen mass transfer in bioreactors? Increased viscosity reduces the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa) by promoting bubble coalescence, slowing bubble rise velocity, and thickening the liquid film resistance at the gas-liquid interface. The result is impaired oxygen supply to cells, which risks dissolved oxygen limitation and reduced cell productivity. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage. This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa). The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel. Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration. Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises. Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. Impeller-to-vessel diameter ratio (D/T) is another variable that must be revisited for high-viscosity applications. Published engineering guidance for animal cell culture places the standard D/T range between 0.33 and 0.5, and moving toward the upper end of that range can significantly improve mixing time and reduce zone heterogeneity in viscous cultures. As culture viscosity rises, torque demand increases nonlinearly, so the mechanical drive system must be specified with adequate torque capacity, validated against the worst-case viscosity expected at peak cell density before committing to a vessel configuration.
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has moved from a research tool into a practical engineering resource for bioreactor scale-up, and its value is particularly high for high-viscosity applications where empirical correlations developed for low-viscosity systems can mislead. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth.
For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. A mass-transfer modeling study in Biochemical Engineering Journal demonstrated that this approach enabled direct scale-up of a CHO antibody process from 2-L to 1,500-L without intermediate steps, with consistent process performance and product quality across scales.
Biochemical Engineering Journal
The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start.
process intensification and continuous bioprocessing
Maintaining dissolved oxygen above the critical threshold becomes progressively more difficult as culture viscosity rises and kLa declines. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. The standard dissolved oxygen control cascade, which increases agitation speed and then increases airflow rate as DO falls, remains the primary control strategy but must be implemented with culture-specific limits to prevent shear damage or excessive CO₂ accumulation from high gas flow rates.
Oxygen enrichment of the inlet gas stream (substituting pure oxygen or high-oxygen mixtures for air) is a widely used supplemental strategy for maintaining DO in high-density, high-viscosity cultures. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in the sparged gas, enrichment increases the driving force for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid interface without requiring a proportional increase in gas flow rate, which would otherwise strip CO₂ and drive pH excursions. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone.

Microspargers (spargers with very small pore sizes that generate fine bubbles) increase the gas-liquid interfacial area and improve kLa in viscous cultures, but are more prone to fouling and require higher inlet pressure to overcome surface tension effects at the pore. Combining a microsparger for oxygen transfer with a ring sparger for CO₂ stripping is an approach used in some high-density culture systems to address both gas transfer directions independently.
Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses is a system-level engineering challenge that requires integrating rheological characterization, impeller selection, drive system specification, dissolved oxygen control strategy, and CFD-guided scale-up into a coherent process development program. The teams that manage this challenge successfully treat mixing as a first-class process parameter from the earliest stages of intensified process design, rather than as a scale-up problem to be solved after the biological performance has been locked in. For programs moving toward commercial manufacturing, the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities provides a framework for integrating these mixing specifications into facility design from the outset.
blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities
The increasing adoption of high-density fed-batch and continuous perfusion platforms, and the insights that connect those approaches to the wider discipline of bioprocessing scale-up , make high-viscosity mixing engineering a near-universal challenge for modern biomanufacturing. Investing in rigorous mixing characterization and physically validated CFD modeling during process development is the most reliable way to prevent agitation failures from appearing at commercial scale, where inadequate agitation means lost batches, failed DO control, and irreproducible scale-up.

Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses refers to the agitation strategies and engineering approaches used to maintain homogeneous culture conditions (including nutrient distribution, dissolved oxygen, and pH uniformity) when culture broth rheology departs from standard low-viscosity conditions due to high cell densities, concentrated feeds, or accumulated metabolites. Why does high cell density increase culture viscosity? Elevated cell density increases the volumetric fraction of suspended biomass in the culture medium and promotes the accumulation of extracellular proteins, polysaccharides, and metabolic byproducts that collectively raise apparent viscosity. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior emerges when these components interact with shear forces during agitation. How does viscosity affect oxygen mass transfer in bioreactors? Increased viscosity reduces the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa) by promoting bubble coalescence, slowing bubble rise velocity, and thickening the liquid film resistance at the gas-liquid interface. The result is impaired oxygen supply to cells, which risks dissolved oxygen limitation and reduced cell productivity.
